lines.text: I've had 2 school tours today, grade 4 classes. I just want to let you know that we saved summer holidays by resolution. So we're all good to go for the next couple of months. At this time, I'd like to give the opening to Councillor Damian Penner.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mayor. Well, the streets are cleaned, the stages have been taken down, and our stomachs are still reeling from the gluttony we subjected them to over this last weekend. at Summer in the City. Even the weather decided to cooperate for almost the entirety of the weekend, and aside from a few gusts of winds that sent some vendors scrambling to catch their tumbling tents, I think overall we can chalk this year's festival down as another tremendous success. In my time spent on the street at our business's booth, I get the opportunity to talk to a variety of people— citizens of Steinbach, visitors from other parts of the province, various food vendors, and of course all the amazing volunteers that help this festival be one of the most successful annual summer festivals in Manitoba. Just to add, those aren't my words. Those are the words from a lot of the vendors around. So very good job. Every year I get to see firsthand the positive impact that this festival has on our community. There's one time specifically that I enjoy the most over the weekend, though, and that is the early morning on Saturday before the streets start filling up. It gives you an entirely different perspective of the city being on Main Street without any cars around. The birds usually singing and the lingering excitement of the night before, matched with the beauty and peace of an empty Main Street. The Wonder Show staff are still eating their breakfasts, and aside from a couple food vendors getting prepared for a busy day and the odd skateboarder enjoying being able to carve a path down an empty roadway, it is peaceful. I found it fitting that yesterday a Steinbach citizen reached out, [name withheld], who sent me a poem she wrote about summer in the city that she asked if I could share with you. So the poem goes, Today at Dawn. Today at dawn, I saw Mr. Jackrabbit at the fair. Before the wheels turned or people folks woke, he hopped and he skipped to a light melody wafting in from the heart of the wood, a crescendo developing from the morning bird band inspired Mr. Rabbit at dawn. He dipped and he dopped, he circled and hopped while dew lay on the ground. While he circled and hopped, he dipped and dopped, his way right out of town. I saw him bow and tip his hat as he slipped 'neath the evergreen grove and disappeared into another world. Into that other world he vanished, where moss and fern cover spread. It is there that he'll bounce and jump on the beds all arranged for rabbits to play. He'll dance to the tunes in those needlework walls till its green frosted ceilings cathedral the sky and its timber pillar and posts cast evening shadows around. The adrenaline will fade as the rabbits partake of one last bedtime hide-and-seek game. And when the sun shuts the grove's twinkling lights, a calm will pervade that cool forest glade while all is scurry and noise at the fair. Yes, today at dawn I saw Mr. Jackrabbit at the fair, but nary a thought could explain the fun that was fought without ticket bought so deep in the heart of the wood. I found this poem a fitting juxtaposition to the hustle and bustle that is any festival. There are the bright lights, the loud horns and sirens, the booming bass of the band rocking, the screams and screeches of delight from children, and of course, being located every year beside the merry-go-round, my personal favorite, the high-pitched tinging carnival sounds on repeat. But at the end of the festival, It isn't the rides you rode, the food you ate, or the bands you listened to that you reflect on. It is the conversations you had and the relationships you built, or perhaps even rekindled over the weekend. Summer in the City is the festival that wakes up our city from the doldrums of winter and gets us looking forward to the hot summer ahead and the friends and family that we connected with at the festival to make plans with in the coming weeks. And as we all cleared the street and vanished into our worlds, I would like to say a big thank you to every volunteer, the city staff, the summer and the city board, and everyone that helped make this another successful festival. Thank you, Mr. Mayor.

Now, what we have here is a situation where the structure has already been built. lines.speaker: Roger Storoschuk
lines.title: Assessor
lines.label: Roger Storoschuk (Assessor, Manitoba Municipal Relations - Assessment Services)
lines.text: I'll just get right into page 1. And this report will provide council with, with an overview of the impact of the reassessment of 2025 in your municipality.

lines.speaker: Roger Storoschuk
lines.title: Assessor
lines.label: Roger Storoschuk (Assessor, Manitoba Municipal Relations - Assessment Services)
lines.text: For 2025, the assessed values of all properties will be updated to a reference date of April 1st, 2023 market values from April 1st, 2021 market values. Properties assessments were last updated in 2023. How do we establish market value for reassessments? First one is to review cost information that we collect over a 2-year cycle. Review sales data. So we review sales information that is deemed to be market value. So essentially willing buyers and willing sellers. And then we also review income information for revenue-bearing properties. Whether it's strip malls or apartments or motels or hotels, regional malls, we do review their income information. So everything that we report today is really based on what is happening in the market and is essentially being set— Thank you. By your ratepayers or your, uh, clients in your municipality. We're simply just reporting back what we found in the last 2 years. This report will provide details on how taxable assessments have changed in your, in your municipality and across the province, and how reassessment 2025 will impact municipal and school taxes. Uh, impacts in this report reflect 2025 modeling. Some assessment changes, uh, could still occur in your municipality that affect actual impacts. So as an example, one of your major projects, well, actually 2 of your major projects that you do have in the City of Steinbach right now would obviously be the event center, even though it's maybe not necessarily a taxable impact, but as well as the Penco corporate headquarters, which will have a substantial assessment that will change your assessment base for 2025. Objectives of reassessing properties. Include equity. All properties across the province are regularly reassessed to ensure assessments keep pace with changing market conditions. Fairness. Property taxes are paid according to the market value of your property. Keeping assessments current is one way to ensure everyone pays their fair share of taxes. And also provide a greater ratepayer understanding. Updating assessments makes it easier for property owners to understand and evaluate their assessments. Page 2 is probably the most important page of the report. The reassessment reflects how property values have changed since the last reassessment. They can be attributed to a combination of changes to supply and demand for real estate, new construction, as well as improvements to existing properties. The province's taxable assessment has increased by $13.2 billion or 13% to $111.2 billion, up from $98 billion last reassessment. Your municipality's taxable assessment has increased by $158 million or 13% To $1.4 billion, and that's up from $1.242 billion, sorry, in 2024. Changes in your municipality's taxable assessment by property class. Single-family residential saw an increase of 15.7%. Apartments saw an increase of 5.7%. Condominiums, so apartment-style or residential-style condominiums, saw an increase of 11.2%. Thank you. For a total average increase for residential property is 14.2%. Farm property, although limited in the city of Steinbach, saw an increase of 22.4%. Commercial and industrial property saw an average increase of 10.4%. Institutional property, which would be your schools, your churches, your hospitals, saw an increase of 6.9%. Pipeline property saw an increase of 21%. Thank you. And designated recreational property, which would be the golf course in the City of Steinbach, saw an increase of 6.8%. This leads to a total average increase of 12.7% across the City of Steinbach. Some additional numbers. There were, based on April 1st, 2000— sorry, April 2nd, 2021 to April 1st, 2023, there are approximately 1,158 sales. Thank you. Of that, approximately 922 were single-family residential sales, 12 multi-residential sales, which will include land, some land transactions as well as land and building transactions, 137 residential condominium sales, 7 properties with farm class on it, and also 76 properties with other property, which is typically associated to commercial. Thank you. Moving on to page 3, uh, I will give a brief rundown of this page, uh, and then just kind of explains how the tax will impact— how this will affect potential property taxes going forward. Assessment increases, decreases resulting from assessment do not necessarily mean increases and decreases. So one common phone call we get is, my assessment went up 25%, my taxes are going to go up 25%, and I can't afford that. That, that's not necessarily how it works. So we'll get into greater detail of that, but that's just one misconception that we do hear on a regular basis. Property assessment simply provides the basis of distributing taxes among your property owners. So the assessment office creates the assessment base, the city establishes their budget and carries forward with their day. Tax and mill rates are set by council for municipal levies, school divisions per Uh, special levies, and the provincial, uh, government sets the education support levy. Shifting of 3 taxes— of these, uh, sorry, of the 3 tax levies occurs between and within property classes when property assessments increase or decrease relative to the average on a municipal, school division, and provincial-wide basis. Only properties seeing above-average increases will likely have an increase in taxes. Uh, the impact of the reassessment 2025 on property taxes Uh, in your municipality is shown on the following pages. Impacts do not take into account other taxes levied on a part of your municipality. I'll focus on probably just the general municipal levy. Property tax impacts have been calculated using the following methodology. A baseline for the municipal tax was determined by first applying the 2023 tax levels against the 2024 assessment to estimate the 2024 general municipal levy. For estimated 2025 general municipal taxes, the general mill rates were recalculated to raise the same amount of tax on the 2025 assessment. So essentially what we're saying, we estimated your budget for 2024, we're going to assume that that budget hasn't changed for 2025. Now I understand that's maybe not the most realistic, uh, scenario, but it does just give an idea of what does reassessment do To the general taxpayer. I won't spend a lot of time on page 4 because it does include the school tax portion of it. I think page 5 is much more beneficial to each and every one of you. And that table below illustrates how municipal levy of each class of your property in your municipality is impacted by reassessment 2025. So based— keep in mind, actually the bottom 2 bullet points are probably the most important when we're reviewing the table. Properties with an assessment increase less than 12.7% should see a municipal tax decrease. Properties with an assessment increase greater than 12.7% should see a m— uh, municipal tax increase. And this is on page 5, just in case. So again, assuming the budget stays the same between the 2 tax years, we would typically see anyone below the average per— or average increase of 12.7% would see A decrease. So how does that affect the tax change? We'd see a small shift to single-family residential of 2.7%, a shift to farm properties at 8.6%, and a 7.4% shift to pipeline properties. Apartments, condos, commercial industrial properties, institutional properties, and recreational properties would see a shift away from them. Thank you. Thank you. Page 6 includes some council's options to moderate impacts. I won't touch on this today. You have a great city manager that is familiar with these possible options as well as municipal services. Overall, the percentage changes aren't drastic compared to some of our other municipalities that we are seeing that Uh, but I've been a part of assessment for 17 years and I haven't seen anyone, uh, take up any of these options. So I'll just move forward to page 7. The provincial, uh, property tax reduction. So the, the most important bullet of page 7 is bullet number 1, the Manitoba school tax rebate for 2024. Owners of residential and farm properties will receive a 50% rebate of their education property taxes applied directly to the property tax statement. So in years past, you may remember you've gotten your tax bill, a couple weeks later you get a check from the government. That check has now officially been eliminated. The reduction is automatically placed on your tax bill. So soon, I'm not sure when tax bills are going out in the City of Steinbach, you will see your typical homeowner's rebate and then you'll see another mat to a school Tax rebate on that bill. Owners of properties will receive— owners of other properties, so again, most typically commercial properties, will receive a 10% rebate of their education property taxes applied directly to their property tax statement. And we do have a couple links available to you for further information. Moving on to page 8. Ratepayers. So I guess one important aspect that I failed to mention today is that assessment notices for the City of Steinbach have hit the mail stream as of today. So we expect probably, well, some maybe even tomorrow, but we expect by the end of the week that residents, property owners in the City of Steinbach will have their assessment notice for 2025. Ratepayers have been informed or can receive additional information about reassessment 2025 in the following ways. A provincial website providing property assessments, maps, and answers to frequently asked questions is available. Anyone with internet access will be able to obtain this information. There is a lot of public information available free of charge. My Property Manitoba is something that the government's been pretty excited about rolling out to the public. I've actually just signed up for the service. Essentially, it can now access and receive their assessment notices and detailed property assessment information online with your account. Thank you. This will eliminate in some cases, so in my case I won't receive an assessment notice in the mail anymore. I will just get it by email. So a toll-free customer service line is available for ratepayers to contact their local assessment office, and that's here in Steinbach, and speak to an assessor. The toll-free number is provided on both the assessment notice and the assessment brochure. Assessment facts are also available, which is a series of informational sheets providing details about property assessment in Manitoba. Have been made available at local assessment sessions. I don't believe the City of Steinbach has used the open house platform. No. Okay, I won't touch on that. And also, municipal administrators also do play an important role, so I can only imagine that we actually don't hear as many phone calls and inquiries as we get. I'm assuming that your staff here at the city office have probably dealt with some of them before they even get to our office. So that is everything for today. Is there any questions?

lines.label: Cindy Rempel Patrick (Board co-chair, Southeast Cancer Support Services Inc.)
lines.text: And that's an incredible amount of trips that were either done by family members or they were done by volunteer drivers and that they were assisted with. And also there was 251 new patients that came up this year. Thank you. So to the existing patients that were in that center, 251. So cancer is, it's increasing, it's affecting more people all the time. There was 31 patients they could provide lymphedema treatments to, 100 patients they provided skin screening treatments that needed it. They brought the devices and diagnostics into the city so people could be tested there, 'cause skin cancer is on the rise. There was 19 clients who they provided wigs. Thank you. So there is definitely a need. And when we compare their community and our community, there's so many similarities, and I just feel that this is a good projection of what we can expect to see besides the transportation program, all the other programs they'll be running. They run between 12 and 15 other programs in addition to transportation, and that consumes nearly 60% of their budget. So the program The money that's raised, that money, 60% of it goes directly to the cancer patients. And that's a high number. And we're glad to see that that amount is just in the transportation program. They've never turned away one patient or a family member who required some form of financial, emotional, or physical assistance. And that is success. And that's what we will aspire to do. And we will do everything we can do to make sure that access to Cancer healthcare will not be denied in our city and in our region in this— in these services. And our proposed budget, we've been working with them, so we have looked at their budgets and their growth, and we have used that as a— as our gauge. And so we show 58% of our budget, of every dollar raised, is going to go directly to the cancer patient who lives in this city or this region. So as she explained, As I explained, it's the first phase and we will expand. There are many expenses involved in our— in a cancer journey that, like she says, our medical system does not cover. And we do need a facility and we do need a place to set up and to be able to provide this. We need to create awareness so people can get this help and then also for people who want to volunteer and contribute. So it's a real community effort. It says community all over. And it's very, very beneficial. Many of us in this room, as Heather said, and you would have resources. You might have family members that live here and friends that can drive you in. But we just heard of the dad from La Broquerie who's sleeping on his daughter's couch in Winnipeg for 6 weeks because he had no access to Winnipeg. And the gentleman from Vassar who is not having any treatment. 'cause he can't get to Steinbach. And it just seems unacceptable. It's just, in our day and age, and in our community, we have a very generous community, and we have a very giving people in the region, and we just feel that if people knew about these needs, they would respond. We've received enormous support since we started this in March, our fundraising campaign in March, and we accepted a challenge from Bethesda Foundation to raise a significant amount of money of pledges for the next 5 years so that it would ensure that we are sustainable. And we have to raise that in the next 90 days. And so we are working hard. It's been very challenging, but we are— we're very confident that we can do it. So we're coming to you as one of our supporters to get us off the ground. Cancer is here. It's increasingly affecting Affecting more lives, and so we need to start now.
